title: The ship from Macao
learnerQuestion: What did the yearly ship from Macao carry to Japan and bring back, who told us so, and how far from the ship were they standing?
sensitiveContentNotice: One part of this Story, "The people on the ship", describes the buying and carrying away of people from Japan, children among them, and deaths at sea.

paragraphs.text: In 1590 the Jesuits printed a book in Latin at their house in Macao.
The bishop's licence to print it had been signed there on 5 September 1589.
It is written as a conversation among three Japanese speakers, Michael, Leo and Linus.
Its title page says it was gathered from the journal of the Japanese envoys to Rome and put into Latin by a Jesuit, Duarte de Sande.
So it is a Jesuit book in Japanese voices. It is not the envoys' own testimony.
Among much else it describes a trade: silk and gold going to Japan, and silver coming into China.
Most of what Europe knew of that trade was written by men who never saw Macao. Who they were, where they stood, and what they left out, is the Story.
A Venetian merchant, Cesare Federici, went to Malacca in 1566 and wrote that he went no further east.
He was told that the Portuguese had built a small town called Macao, with a church and houses of wood.
The customs, he was told, belonged to the king of China and were paid at Canton.
Historians date the settlement to the 1550s: an understanding with officials at Canton in 1554, and leave to settle at Macao in 1557.
A Dutchman, Jan Huygen van Linschoten, lived in Goa from 1583 to 1589 and never reached China.
He wrote, from what he heard there, that Portuguese and Chinese people lived in Macao together and traded with the men of Canton.
The Portuguese could buy at Canton. They could not stay.
Ralph Fitch, an Englishman at Malacca in 1588, wrote that they had to enter their names in a book at the gate and sleep in their boats outside the city.
Federici and Linschoten were told the same.
Fitch was at Malacca from 8 February to 29 March 1588.
He reported that the Portuguese sent a great ship from Macao to Japan every year, carrying white silk, gold, musk and porcelain.
It brought back, he wrote, nothing but silver.
Linschoten, writing from Goa, said the same: silks went out, and nothing but silver came back.
By his account only one ship a year could sail to Japan, by the king of Portugal's licence.
The whole voyage, from Goa by Malacca and Macao to Japan and back, took at least three years, because the ships waited for the monsoon at each stop.
A modern historian counts more than one ship in many of the years from 1557 to 1590.
Souza's count has two sailings from Macao in 1590, and warns that some of the ships counted were junks, not great carracks.
The captain of the Japan ship, Linschoten wrote from Goa, was also the chief ruler at Macao for as long as he was there, and could gain 150,000 or 200,000 ducats by the voyage.
The crews were not all Portuguese. Linschoten wrote home that a friend from his own province, Dirck Gerritsz of Enkhuizen, had gone to China and Japan as a ship's gunner.
The port the ship used in Japan was Nagasaki. A Japanese historian writes that it was opened in 1570.
Fitch and Linschoten wrote of silk and silver. They did not write of this.
The ship that carried silver back to Macao also carried people who had been bought in Japan.
We know it from the Church's own papers. No one carried on the ship left an account that we have read.
None of these papers is dated to 1590. One is from three years earlier and one from eight years later. Both describe something that happened year after year.
On 24 July 1587 Hideyoshi, the ruler of Japan, sent the head of the Jesuits in Japan a list of charges.
One of them, in a letter of the Jesuit Luís Fróis printed in 1598, was that the Portuguese bought many Japanese people and carried them away as captives to their own lands.
The Jesuit superior answered that the Portuguese bought them because other Japanese sold them, and that the Fathers were grieved by it and could not stop it.
On 4 September 1598 the bishop of Japan and the Jesuit superiors met at Nagasaki and set down what they knew.
Their record says that a great number of Japanese were sold to the Portuguese every year.
It says those sold were boys and girls, children among them, and that most had been tricked or taken by force.
It says that Portuguese of every rank bought as many as they could.
And it says that many died on the voyage to Macao, because they were packed one on top of another.
The record says sellers made them tell the buyers they had been taken in a lawful war, and threatened to kill them if they refused.
Once they were free of the threat, it says, they told the whole truth. It does not give their words.

The churchmen wrote that their own side had taken part. The late bishop had given licences to take bought boys and girls out of Japan, and Jesuit Fathers had advised and signed papers binding them to years of service.
They wrote that they had thought it the lesser of two evils. The meeting resolved to forbid all of it.

Hideyoshi had already forbidden it, on pain of death. The record says Japanese sellers and brokers were put to death at Nagasaki, among them the master of the boat the Portuguese used to reach their ship.
Some of those carried lived on in Macao. The record says some had sold themselves to get there and then fled into China.
It says boys set free in Macao with nothing turned to robbing Chinese farmers on their way to market.

beats.sensitiveNotice: This part describes people bought in Japan and carried to Macao, children among them. Many died on the voyage.

paragraphs.text: The Ming court had cut off trade with Japan.
When it reopened sea trade to its own merchants in 1567, it kept the ban on Japan.
Chinese merchants still traded with Japan against the ban. But a historian of Chinese money writes that Portuguese ships from Macao were the main route by which Japanese silver reached China.
Japan had the silver. Its boom began in the 1530s, with rich finds at Iwami and a refining method that came by way of Korea.
And Japan wanted silk. A Jesuit who lived there from 1577 wrote that silk had been rare when he arrived, and that under Hideyoshi even farmers and their wives came to wear it.

Gold went on the same ship, because it bought more silver in Japan. In the later sixteenth century one tael of gold was worth about seven or eight taels of silver in China, and about ten in Japan. A tael was a Chinese weight of about 37.5 grams.
The Macao book has a Japanese speaker say he heard that one ship, 'this present year', carried 2,000 loaves of Chinese gold to Japan.
The book was licensed in 1589, so the year meant is 1589 or earlier. A modern historian calls the cargo scarcely credible.
The same book says Portuguese merchants carried silver into Canton every year, and that almost none came out again.
Inside Japan, a Japanese historian records silver sent to Hideyoshi as tribute from the mines, and Iwami silver cast into coin for his army in Korea in the 1590s.
An economist has argued that the mines' profits are what let one lord unify Japan. He calls this a hypothesis for specialists to test.
How much silver came back? No one counted it at the time.
Fitch, at Malacca, was told that the ship brought above 600,000 cruzados in silver every year, and that the Portuguese spent it in China with 200,000 more from India.
That is a figure he was given, eighteen hundred miles from Macao. It is the one most historians start from.
A modern historian, George Bryan Souza, counted the years in which a ship sailed. He estimates that the Portuguese took 7.5 to 8.9 million taels of silver out of Japan between 1580 and 1597.
He built that on Kobata's estimate of 500,000 to 600,000 taels a year, about 18,700 to 22,500 kilograms. Kobata had built his on the figures of Fitch and two Jesuits.
So the modern total is the old reports multiplied by the years of sailing. It is not a separate count, and Souza himself calls his data far from perfect.
Kobata, the Japanese historian of the mines, wrote that Japan's output in these years cannot now be calculated.
A later historian, Kent Deng, warns that European traders almost certainly mixed Japanese silver with silver from elsewhere, so the same silver can be counted twice.
Historians say that from the 1530s until at least the 1570s Japan was China's main source of foreign silver.
Von Glahn estimates that about 60 per cent of the silver China imported in the second half of the century came from Japan, and calls his total a minimum.
That is the mainstream account, and it is an interpretation. The Claim beneath each sentence says whose voice it rests on.

**Not yet researched.** This Story stops at Macao about 1590. What the silver did inside China, what the silk did inside Japan, where the people carried from Japan were taken after Macao, and how Chinese and Japanese ships came to carry this trade themselves have not been researched, so none is offered as a researched path. When a path is researched, it will appear here with its own Claims and Evidence.

warnings.name: Evidence concentrated in colonial Sources
warnings.text: No European who described this trade saw Macao. On the people carried, every Source is a churchman writing about his own side.

The chapter number is taken from its table numbering, 4.1 to 4.6; we do not hold the contents page.
